en: Konow, Sten: *Central Asian Fragments of the Aṣṭādaśasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā and of an Unidentified Text*, Calcutta 1942 (*Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India*, 69).
= AṣṭāK; unidentified = Praj(U1)
Bidyabinod, B. B.: “Fragment of a Prajñāpāramitā Manuscript from Central Asia,” *Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India* 32 (1927), pp. 1–11. = AṣṭāB AṣṭāH = 1 folio from S. Hedin.
Edited by H. Smith in Montell, G.: *Sven Hedin's Archaeological Collections from Khotan*, 2 vols.
Stockholm 1938 and also in Konow (AṣṭāK, A fol. 97) recto.

1. There is the concentration called "the convergence of all that is without conflict and with conflict"; the concentration called "delighting in being without abode like the wind"; the concentration called "mindless and established in suchness"; the concentration called "crushing the defilement of the body"; the concentration called "like space, destroying the defilement of speech and uprooting it";
and the concentration called "unattached, liberated, and unstained like space. These, friend Śāradvatīputra, are the concentrations of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, in which indeed [they abide].
The bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
as well as other immeasurable and incalculable gateways of meditative concentration and gateways of mnemonic formulas,
training in which bodhisattvas mahāsattvas [attain these goals].
They quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the venerable Śāradvatīputra: "O friend Śāradvatīputra, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has indeed been prophesied for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by the Arhats and Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past; and those who are [prophesied] now..."
In world systems in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently reside and maintain themselves;
those Tathāgatas also now bestow prophecies upon that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who dwells in these samādhis yet does not perceive any samādhi whatsoever.
And by means of these concentrations, he does not conceive: "These other bodhisattvas have not entered meditative attainment;
I, however, have entered, am entering, and will enter."

Indeed, none of those discursive thoughts exist for him, nor do they arise. When this had been said, the venerable Śāradvatīputra addressed the venerable Subhūti as follows: "In that case, friend Subhūti, does a bodhisattva, while established in those samādhis..."

That great being should be known as having been prophesied by the Tathāgatas of the past, as well as by those Tathāgatas who currently reside in the world-systems of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā.
They maintain themselves. He said:

"No, friend Śāradvatīputra. "For what reason? "Because, friend Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom is not one thing, samādhi another, and the bodhisattva mahāsattva yet another. The bodhisattva is indeed samādhi; samādhi is indeed the bodhisattva. Both samādhi and the bodhisattva are the perfection of wisdom. He said:

"Friend Subhūti, if the samādhi is not one thing and the bodhisattva another— such that the samādhi itself is the bodhisattva and the bodhisattva himself is the samādhi— and if both that samādhi and that bodhisattva are indeed the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā),
then he does not know the equality of all phenomena (sarvadharmasamatā) by means of that samādhi, nor does he perceive it."
He said: "By this very method,
friend Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not cognize that equality of all phenomena through that samādhi."
Nor does he perceive it. For what reason? It is said:
because that bodhisattva, that samādhi, and that perfection of wisdom are simply non-existent, he neither knows nor perceives them.
Then the Blessed One gave his approval to the venerable Subhūti, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!

Well-spoken are these words, just as you were designated by me as the foremost of the disciples who dwell in non-contention (*araṇā-vihārin*). This instruction is worthy of you; and thus should a bodhisattva mahāsattva [practice] in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)."
One should train while practicing in this way regarding the perfection of meditation and the perfection of vigor.
One should train in the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity.
In this way, one should train in the foundations of mindfulness,
up to the noble eightfold path and the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
[The passage continues] as far as: "one should train in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Then the Venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, when training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom."
The Blessed One said:
"Śāradvatīputra, when training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom,
and that by means of non-apprehension."
In this way, up to training in the perfection of generosity—
and so forth—
training in this manner, he trains in the foundations of mindfulness.
To the extent that one trains in this way, up to training in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
it is by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.

Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, when training in this way, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in the perfection of wisdom by means of the yoga of non-apprehension?
The Blessed One replied:
"Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way trains in the perfection of wisdom by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.
He asked: "Venerable Blessed One, what is it that he does not apprehend?"
The Blessed One said:
"One does not perceive a self; one does not perceive a sentient being."
As long as one does not perceive that which knows and sees—
on account of its absolute purity—
one likewise does not perceive the aggregates or the elements.
For one does not apprehend the sense bases,
because they are absolutely pure;
likewise, one does not apprehend ignorance, up to and including old age and death.
Based on absolute purity; thus [it is said].
(AṣṭāK, A fol. 98) Recto.
One does not apprehend suffering;
one does not apprehend the origin, cessation, or the path,
by virtue of their absolute purity.
In this way, one does not apprehend the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm,
by virtue of their utter purity;
likewise, one does not apprehend the applications of mindfulness.
As long as one does not perceive the noble eightfold path on account of its ultimate purity,
likewise one does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
One does not apprehend the qualities of a Buddha,
by virtue of their ultimate purity;
one does not apprehend the six perfections.
Based on ultimate purity,
one does not apprehend a stream-enterer; based on ultimate purity,
one likewise does not apprehend a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat.

“By virtue of ultimate purity, one does not apprehend a pratyekabuddha, one does not apprehend a bodhisattva, and one does not apprehend a tathāgata—by virtue of ultimate purity. Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Blessed One, what is that purity? The Blessed One replied:
"The non-arising of all dharmas is likewise their non-cessation, non-defilement, non-purification, non-manifestation, non-apprehension, and non-conditioning; this is the purity of all dharmas.
He said: "Furthermore, Blessed Lord, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way..."
"In which dharmas has the Blessed One trained? The Blessed One said:
"Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, he has not trained in any dharmas at all.
Why is that? Because, Śāradvatīputra, these [dharmas]..."
These eight dharmas exist in such a way that these foolish ordinary people are attached to them. He asked:
"But how, Venerable Blessed One, do these dharmas exist?"
"For just as these foolish common people are attached," the Blessed One said,
"so do they not exist."
They do not exist in that way;
for it is because they do not exist in such a manner that they are called "ignorance" (avidyā).
He said:
"Venerable Blessed One, why is it said that ignorance does not exist?
The Blessed One replied,
"Śāradvatīputra, form does not exist, by way of internal emptiness."
Up to and including the emptiness of the nature of non-existence,
in this way feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist,
[beginning] with internal emptiness.

11. From [the first] up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*): in this way, the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) do not exist. [The same applies to the following items. Pe-yā-laṃ.
Up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), they do not exist,
by reason of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the nature of non-existence.

Wherein foolish ordinary people, under the power of ignorance, are attached to craving and hope, and by them knowledge is imagined; being overwhelmed by ignorance, they are stuck in both extremes— namely, the extremes of annihilation and eternalism— and they neither know nor see.
And those phenomena which do not exist, they conceptualize;
having conceptualized them, they become attached to name-and-form, and so forth.
3. As long as they remain attached to the eighteen unshared attributes of a Buddha, they conceptualize dharmas that do not exist;
yet they neither know nor see them.

Do they not know, do they not see form? They do not know, they do not see the unique [unshared] qualities. Likewise, they do not know, they do not see feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
...and so on, up to: they do not know and do not see the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
and because they do not know and do not awaken to them.
They are reckoned as "foolish ordinary persons";
they do not go forth.
Where do they not lead? They do not lead to sovereignty over the desire realm,
nor likewise to the form realm or the formless realm.
They do not set out toward the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
they do not set out toward the dharmas of the bodhisattvas; they do not set out toward the dharmas of the perfectly awakened ones (samyaksaṃbuddha).
And they do not have faith. Why do they not have faith?
They do not have faith in form, nor in the emptiness of form.
In this way, [he contemplates] feeling and the emptiness of feeling; perception and the emptiness of perception; mental formations and the emptiness of mental formations.
They do not have faith in consciousness and the emptiness of consciousness; likewise,
they do not have faith in the Buddha-qualities and the Buddha-qualities.
Furthermore, they do not abide anywhere. Where do they not abide?
They do not abide in the perfection of generosity.
As long as they do not abide in the perfection of wisdom,
they do not abide on the stage of non-retrogression,
and so on, until they do not abide in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
For that reason, they are called "foolish ordinary people" (*bālapṛthagjana*).
Regarding "clinging" (*abhiniveśa*), what is it that these people cling to?
To what are they attached? They are attached to form (*rūpa*), up to and including consciousness (*vijñāna*); likewise, they are attached to the eye (*cakṣus*).
They are attached, even up to being attached to the mind; they are attached to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects;
likewise, they are attached to the elements, attached to passion, hatred, and delusion, attached to views, and attached to the foundations of mindfulness, and so forth.

...up to being attached to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). When this had been said, the Venerable Śāradvatīputra addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Furthermore, Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has newly set out in the vehicle [should train] in the perfection of wisdom..."

While practicing, he would lack skill in means and would not have fallen into the hands of a spiritual friend; he would become afraid, terrified, and fall into a state of dread. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, what is [the lack of skill in means] for a bodhisattva?"

This is the skillful means of the Mahāsattva, wherein a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having heard this teaching while practicing, is not terrified, does not tremble, and does not fall into fear. The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva..."

While practicing the perfection of wisdom, he contemplates form with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects in its aspect of impermanence; yet that [form] is not apprehended at all. In the same way, he contemplates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects in their aspect of impermanence; yet those are not apprehended. Subhūti, this is the skill in means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, contemplates form under the aspect of suffering, yet does not apprehend it at all; likewise [he contemplates] feeling, perception, and mental formations.
1. One examines consciousness by way of its aspect of suffering, yet does not apprehend it;
and so on, one examines form by way of its aspect of selflessness, yet does not apprehend it.
2. Likewise, one examines feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness by way of their aspect of selflessness, yet does not apprehend them.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects,
contemplates form as impermanent and does not apprehend it at all; in the same way, he contemplates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as impermanent.
And he does not apprehend that; [the same applies] in detail: he contemplates form as non-self and does not apprehend that.
Likewise, he contemplates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as non-self and does not apprehend that. He contemplates form as wishless and does not apprehend that.
In this way, he contemplates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as being wishless, yet he does not apprehend them.
Subhūti, this is the skill in means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
While practicing the perfection of generosity, he does not tremble,
he is not terrified, and he does not fall into fear.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom contemplates thus: "Form is empty by way of the emptiness of form; form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form. In the same way, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty; by way of the emptiness of consciousness, consciousness is empty.
Consciousness itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is consciousness.
Likewise, due to the emptiness of the eye, the eye is empty; the eye itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is the eye. It is the same for the ear, the nose, the tongue, and the body.

The mind is empty of the emptiness of the mind; the mind itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is the mind—and so on, up to: the feeling conditioned by eye-contact is empty of the emptiness of the feeling conditioned by eye-contact;

the feeling conditioned by eye-contact is empty, the feeling conditioned by eye-contact itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is the feeling conditioned by eye-contact. Likewise, up to: the feeling conditioned by mind-contact is empty of the emptiness of the feeling conditioned by mind-contact; the feeling conditioned by mind-contact is empty.

Feeling conditioned by mental contact is itself emptiness; emptiness itself is feeling conditioned by mental contact. Likewise, the emptiness of the applications of mindfulness is empty of the applications of mindfulness, and the applications of mindfulness themselves are emptiness;
emptiness itself is the applications of mindfulness—and so on for the rest.
Up to the point that the emptiness of the Buddha-dharmas is such that the Buddha-dharmas are empty;
the Buddha-dharmas themselves are emptiness.

"Emptiness itself is the qualities of a Buddha. For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not tremble, is not terrified, and does not fall into fear.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, who is the spiritual friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
"Whoever, having heard this teaching on the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā-nirdeśa*), is not terrified, does not tremble, and does not fall into fear, is embraced by that [virtuous friend].
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, this is the virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
10. That he teaches the Dharma that form is impermanent, and that by way of non-apprehension;
likewise, he teaches the Dharma that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
And that is by way of non-apprehension;
furthermore, he does not dedicate those roots of goodness to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
Except for omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), this is the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, [this is] the spiritual friend of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
When he teaches the Dharma that form is suffering,
he does so by way of non-apprehension; likewise,
when he teaches the Dharma that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are suffering, he does so by way of non-apprehension.
And those roots of virtue he does not dedicate toward the level of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas,
but rather toward omniscience; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s spiritual friend.
...and so on;
he teaches the Dharma that form is non-self.
Up to and including consciousness;
and that by way of non-apprehension,
he teaches the Dharma through the emptiness of form.
In this way, he teaches the Dharma up to the emptiness of consciousness,
and that by means of non-apprehension;
likewise, he teaches the Dharma through the signlessness of form.
4. He teaches the Dharma by way of the signlessness of consciousness, and that by means of non-apprehension;
likewise, he teaches the Dharma by way of the wishlessness of form.
He teaches the Dharma by way of the wishlessness of consciousness,
and that by means of non-apprehension;
likewise, he teaches the Dharma by way of the tranquility of form and the seclusion of form.
To the extent that he teaches the Dharma through the tranquility of consciousness and the solitude of consciousness,
and by means of non-apprehension;
and those roots of merit as well.

6. One does not dedicate [merit] toward the level of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, but rather toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*); this is the virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, there is another virtuous friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
That which he teaches as the Dharma: "The eye is impermanent," and so on, up to "the mind is impermanent";
and so forth, up to "feeling conditioned by eye-contact is impermanent"—this is the teaching of the Dharma.
He teaches; thus, up to feeling conditioned by mental contact, he teaches the Dharma that it is impermanent,
and that by way of non-apprehension,
as well as those roots of merit.

One does not dedicate [merit] toward the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha, but rather toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*); Subhūti, this is the good friend of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. [The rest is as before.]
"It is suffering," "it is non-self," and so on, up to "it is secluded."
He teaches the Dharma by means of non-apprehension,
and those roots of merit as well.

One does not dedicate [merit] to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha; rather, one dedicates it solely to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Subhūti, this is the good friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore:
Subhūti, the good friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is one who teaches the Dharma for the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness,
up to teaching the Dharma for the seclusion of the applications of mindfulness.
And that [is] in the yoga of non-apprehension.
"It should be rejected.
For what reason?

Because, sir, these perfections were not spoken by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; they are mere poetry, products of poetic invention. Therefore, sir, they should not be heard, nor should they be taken up, nor should they be mastered."
They should not be upheld, nor recited, nor brought to mind, nor taught to others; Subhūti, this should be known as a spiritual friend of evil to a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva—

3. An evil friend is one who does not instruct him in the works of Māra, nor points out the faults of Māra. For instance, O sir, the wicked Māra approaches in the guise of a Buddha and diverts the Bodhisattva from the six perfections, saying: "What to you, sir..."
"Noble son, when this perfection of wisdom has been cultivated in this way,
what need have you for the perfection of meditation? What need have you for the perfection of vigor?"
What is the use of the perfection of patience? What is the use of the perfection of ethical discipline?
What is the use of your cultivation of the perfection of generosity?
5. Subhūti, this should be known as the evil friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, having approached that bodhisattva mahāsattva in the guise of a Buddha, teaches him discourses associated with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, even up to the avadānas and instructions.
He illuminates, analyzes, makes clear,
and fully elucidates these such things as these.
One should know that this is a wicked friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not point out these seven works of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, having approached a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the guise of a Buddha, speaks to him thus:

"O son of good family, you are not a bodhisattva; you do not possess the thought of awakening (bodhicitta); nor are you irreversible, and you will not be able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
Thus,
one who does not point out nor cause another to understand such deeds of Māra as these should be known as a bad friend to the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, having approached a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the guise of a Buddha, speaks to him thus:
"Noble son, the eye is empty of a self or of anything belonging to a self;
likewise, noble son, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind are empty of a self or of anything belonging to a self."
In the same way, noble son, forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are empty of a self or of anything belonging to a self;
and so on, as before.
From feeling conditioned by eye-contact up to feeling conditioned by mind-contact,
they are empty of a self or of anything belonging to a self.
Or likewise, the perfection of giving is empty, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, which is empty of self or of what belongs to a self;
the same applies to the foundations of mindfulness.
Up to the noble eightfold path;
up to the three gateways to liberation, which are empty of self or of anything belonging to a self. In the same way, the ten powers of a Tathāgata [are empty].

"Son of good family, even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty of a self or of anything belonging to a self; what will you do with unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening when you have fully awakened to it?
Thus he speaks to him, failing to point out or instruct him regarding such deeds of Māra.
He does not awaken [one to this].
This should be known as a bad friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore:
Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, having approached a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the guise of a pratyekabuddha, would say this to him:
"O son of good family, the eastern direction is empty of Buddhas, Blessed Ones, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas;
there are no Buddhas, Blessed Ones, here."
5. There are no bodhisattvas and no śrāvakas; as it is in the eastern direction, so it is in all directions throughout the ten quarters and in all world-systems.

Whoever does not point out, does not teach, and does not awaken one to such deeds of Māra—this should be known as a bad friend (pāpamitra) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. 6. This should be known as a bad friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Māra the Evil One, approaching in the guise of a disciple, diverts the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva from mental orientations associated with omniscience;
he instructs him with mental orientations associated with disciples and solitary buddhas.
And he instructs: "One who does not point out, does not teach, and does not awaken one to such deeds of Māra as these should be known as a bad friend to a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One,
approaching in the guise of a preceptor or a teacher, causes a bodhisattva mahāsattva to become alienated from the conduct of a bodhisattva;
he causes him to become alienated from mental attentions associated with omniscience.
He causes [the practitioner] to become detached from the foundations of mindfulness;
and so on, up to causing him to become detached from the noble eightfold path.
He encourages and enjoins them toward emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
"Come, O son of good family! Having cultivated these dharmas, realize the stage of a śrāvaka.
What will you do with unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, when you do not point out such deeds of Māra as these?"
And I must penetrate the single gateway that brings about the realization of all dharmas.
[The full passage] should be repeated as before: "And I must train in all dharmas for the sake of penetrating the immeasurable accomplishment.
These, Subhūti, are [the qualities] of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

2. There are diamond-like productions of the thought of awakening; abiding in these, the bodhisattva mahāsattva will bring about leadership over the great mass of sentient beings by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. Furthermore, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva should thus produce the thought:
He generates [this thought]:

"As many beings as there are—whether those in the hells, or those in the animal realm, or those in the world of Yama—who experience painful sensations, may I experience those sensations for their sake.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should generate this thought: "For the sake of each and every being, may I undergo those sensations of hellish suffering for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons."
Until all those beings have been led to final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder;
by that very means, for the sake of all beings, may I experience those painful sensations of hell for hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of eons, until they [are all exhausted].
"May all six classes of beings be led to final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder.

Only afterwards, having planted roots of merit for my own sake and having accumulated the manifold provisions for enlightenment over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, may I awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Thus [he thought].
Subhūti, this is the diamond-like production of the thought of awakening of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; established in this, he will bring about leadership among the great mass of sentient beings.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should possess a mind that is upright and noble—
the mind by which he shall bring about the state of preeminence for all sentient beings.
In this regard, this is the "preeminent mind" of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

9. Noble mind (*udāracitta*) is that which, from the first production of the thought of awakening (*prathamacittotpāda*) onward, never gives rise to a mind of passion (*rāga*), nor a mind of hatred (*dveṣa*), nor a mind of delusion (*moha*), nor a mind of harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), nor a mind of violence (*hiṃsā*), nor a mind of a disciple (*śrāvaka*), nor a mind of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha*).

10. Subhūti, this is the foremost mind and noble mind of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, by which he will bring about the state of preeminence among all sentient beings; yet by that mind, he does not conceive pride (*na manyate*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must possess an unshakable mind.

In this regard, what is the unshakable nature of the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? It is that, while attending to the mind of omniscience, he does not conceive any conceit on account of it; this, Subhūti, is the unshakable nature of the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should possess a mind of benefit and compassion toward all sentient beings.
In this regard, Subhūti, the mind of compassion for the welfare of all beings belonging to a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows:

namely, that it becomes a protection for all beings and a state of non-abandonment, yet he remains free from conceit because of it. And thus, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, he will be held in the highest esteem by all beings.
And that by means of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should always be one who desires the Dharma and delights in the Dharma.
And by one devoted to the practice of delighting in the Dharma.
In that regard, what is the Dharma which is not destroyed by its own nature, nor is it differentiated, and no differentiation of it can be found?
Whether it be material or immaterial, this is called a phenomenon (dharma).
What is the desire for phenomena?
It is that which [is directed] toward phenomena.
Such aspirations are called the desire for the Dharma.
What is the lack of desire for the Dharma?
What is the lack of cruelty toward qualities within the teachings?
What is delight in the teachings?
It is this: delight and intense delight in the teachings; this is called delight in the teachings. What is the application of the garden of the teachings?
6. Application: That which is the cultivation, practice, mastery, and frequent exercise of that Dharma is called application to the yoga of the delight in the Dharma.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva practicing [the path] should proceed.
A Mahāsattva, when leading a great multitude of beings, should cause them to attain preeminence,
and that by means of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-yoga*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) [should do so] regarding internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*).

Having stood [in the perfections], up to having stood in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, one should exercise leadership over the great mass of sentient beings who are fixed [in the right path],
and that by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by a bodhisattva...

A Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, having established himself in the foundations of mindfulness and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, having established himself in those eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, should, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension, bring about leadership over the great mass of sentient beings who are destined for certainty.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, having established himself in the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) and having established himself in the concentration of liberation that is unattached like space and conditioned phenomena (*ākāśa-saṃskṛta-nirupalepa-vimukti-samādhi*), should, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-yoga*), exercise leadership over the great multitude of sentient beings who are destined for certainty.
Indeed, Subhūti, it is by abiding in these dharmas that [this is to be done].
In the mass of sentient beings, he must be made to attain preeminence. Therefore, he is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
The eleventh chapter, titled "The Chapter on Similes," is completed.
Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Blessed One, it occurs to me as well for what reason a bodhisattva is called a 'mahāsattva'."
The Blessed One said: "Does it occur to you, Śāradvatīputra? He replied: "It occurs to me."
3. "Venerable Blessed One, what did you say?
You teach the Dharma to sentient beings for the sake of abandoning the view of a self;
likewise [you teach it] for the sake of abandoning the view of a sentient being, the view of a person, the view of a living soul, and the view of a nourisher."

4. He teaches the Dharma to sentient beings for the sake of abandoning the view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*), the view of a human (*manuja-dṛṣṭi*), the view of a man (*mānava*), and the views of an agent (*kāraka*), a doer (*kartṛ*), an arouser (*utthāpaka*), an instigator (*samutthāpaka*), an experiencer (*vedaka*), a knower (*jñātṛ*), and a seer (*darśaka*).
Likewise, he does so for the sake of abandoning the views of annihilationism (*uccheda*) and eternalism (*śāśvata*).

5. He teaches the Dharma to sentient beings for the sake of abandoning the view of existence (*asti-dṛṣṭi*), the view of non-existence (*nāsti-dṛṣṭi*), the view of the aggregates (*skandha-dṛṣṭi*), the view of the elements (*dhātu-dṛṣṭi*), the view of the truths (*satya-dṛṣṭi*), and the view of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dṛṣṭi*).

Likewise, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings for the sake of their abandonment, [possessing] the vision of the foundations of mindfulness up to the vision of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
likewise, the vision of maturing sentient beings, the vision of purifying the buddha-field, the vision of awakening, and the vision of the Buddha.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is so called because he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings for the sake of abandoning the view of turning the wheel of Dharma;
furthermore, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings for the sake of abandoning the view of final nirvana.
He teaches; for that reason, he is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Venerable Śāradvatīputra: "Friend Śāradvatīputra, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva teaches the Dharma to sentient beings for the sake of abandoning these views..."
"For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva have a view of form? Likewise, why does he have a view of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness? [And so on]...
up to why does he have a view of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
When this had been said, the venerable Śāradvatīputra spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "In this regard, friend Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while in the perfection of wisdom..."
11. Practicing without skill in means, having apprehended form, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension.
Likewise, having apprehended feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, one gives rise to a view by way of apprehension.
[The same] as before, up to: not having apprehended the eighteen unshared qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), one gives rise to a view by means of apprehension (*upalambha-yogena*).
For this reason, friend Subhūti, a bodhisattva who is unskilled in means (*anupāya-kuśala*) comes to have a view of form (*rūpa-dṛṣṭi*).
[2] The same applies in detail, up until: there arises the view that the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are [perceptible].

Therein, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, skilled in means, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, through skill in means teaches the Dharma to sentient beings for the sake of abandoning these views by way of non-apprehension. [3]

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, it occurs to me as well as to what purpose a bodhisattva is called a 'mahāsattva'. The Blessed One said: "Does it occur to you, Subhūti? Subhūti said:

"It occurs to me, Venerable Blessed One, that the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is a thought equal to the unequaled, a thought not shared by any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; for that reason, he is called a 'bodhisattva mahāsattva.
For what reason? Because, Venerable Blessed One, that thought of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatācitta*) is untainted (*anāsrava*) and not included within the three realms (*traidhātuka*)."
Furthermore, O Noble One, although the mind of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā-citta*) is untainted (*anāsrava*) and not included within the three realms (*traidhātuka*),
he is nonetheless unattached even to that mind; therefore, he is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the venerable Subhūti:

"Subhūti, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind that is equal to the unequaled, the mind that is not shared with any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas? When he had been addressed in this way, the venerable Subhūti said this to the venerable Śāradvatīputra:
8. Here, venerable Śāradvatīputra, from the first production of the thought of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive the arising or the cessation of any dharma whatsoever,
nor does he perceive any dharma as undergoing diminution.
Or it undergoes increase;
nor does the defilement or purification of any dharma whatsoever exist.
And in that, Reverend Śāradvatīputra, where there is neither arising nor cessation, neither decrease nor increase, neither defilement nor purification—there [is such a state].
Neither the mind of a śrāvaka, nor the mind of a pratyekabuddha, nor the mind of a bodhisattva, nor the mind of a perfectly awakened buddha.

"Therefore, friend Śāradvatīputra, the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is an unequaled and equal mind, an uncommon mind—unshared with all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "As for what you have said, friend Subhūti:"
Therein also, [there is] the mind of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
(AṣṭāB, Pl. I, 1/2) recto

The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, personally enters into the meditative absorptions through skill in means, yet he is not reborn under their influence; furthermore, he establishes others in the meditative absorptions. This is..."
"Subhūti, this is the perfection of meditation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, what is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? "Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, does not adhere to any phenomena, [penetrating] the intrinsic nature of all phenomena."

And by means of non-apprehension, he contemplates all phenomena and, through non-attachment to all phenomena and the contemplation of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, he encourages, introduces, and establishes others [in this] by means of non-apprehension; this, Subhūti, is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
This, Subhūti, is the [perfection of wisdom] of a bodhisattva.
This is the Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is as follows: namely, internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of nature, and the emptiness of specific characteristics.

7. The emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*).
Among these, what is internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*)? Internal phenomena (*adhyātmika-dharmāḥ*) are said to be: 8. the eye (*cakṣus*) and the ear (*śrotra*).
The nose, the tongue, and the body.

The mind. In that regard, the eye is empty of the eye, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason? Because this is its very nature. Likewise, the ear is empty of the ear, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason? Because this is its very nature. The nose is empty of the nose, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason? Because this is its very nature.
The tongue is empty of the tongue, by reason of its being neither immutable nor indestructible.
For what reason? Because this is its very nature.

The body is empty of the body, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible; for what reason? This is its very nature. The mind is empty of the mind, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible; for what reason? This is its very nature.
This is called internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*)?
External phenomena are said to be form (*rūpa*).
Sound, odor, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena—among these, form is empty of form, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason? This is its very nature.

Likewise, sound, odor, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena are empty of phenomena, by virtue of their being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason? This is their very nature. This is called external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*).

Now, what is internal-external emptiness (*adhyātmabahirdhā-śūnyatā*)? Internal-external phenomena are said to be the six internal bases (*āyatana*) and the six external bases; these are called internal-external phenomena. Therein, internal phenomena are empty of external [phenomena], by virtue of their being neither immutable nor subject to destruction. [End of page] verso.
For what reason? Because this is their nature: external phenomena are empty of internal phenomena, by virtue of being neither immutable nor subject to destruction.
For what reason? Because this is their nature; this is called "internal-and-external emptiness" (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*).

In that regard, what is the "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*)? That which is the emptiness of all phenomena is empty by virtue of being neither immutable nor subject to destruction; this is called the "emptiness of emptiness."

In that regard, what is great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*)? The eastern direction is empty of the eastern direction; likewise, the southern, western, northern, downward, and upward directions are empty of the upward direction, and the intermediate directions are empty of the intermediate directions, by virtue of their being neither immutable nor subject to destruction. For what reason? Because this is their very nature (*prakṛti*); this is great emptiness. In that regard, what is ultimate emptiness (*paramārthaśūnyatā*)? The ultimate is said to be *nirvāṇa*; therein, *nirvāṇa* is empty of *nirvāṇa*.

Based on its being neither immutable nor subject to destruction. Why is that? Because this is its very nature; this is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). In that regard, what is the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*)? The conditioned is said to be the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Therein, from the realm of desire up to the formless realm, each is empty of itself, based on its being neither immutable nor subject to destruction. This is called the emptiness of the conditioned. In that regard, what is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*)?

7. It is said: that which has no arising, no cessation, no destruction, and no alteration—this is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). In this regard, the unconditioned is empty of the unconditioned, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. 8. For what reason? Because this is its very nature (*prakṛti*).
This is called the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).

In that regard, what is absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*)? It is that dharma for which no absolute arising is perceived. Why is that? Because its intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) is such; this is called absolute emptiness. In that regard, what is the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*)? It is that for which neither a beginning nor an end is perceived. Why is that? Because its intrinsic nature is such; this is called the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end.

10. In that regard, what is the emptiness of non-requital? That wherein there is no requital for any dharma whatsoever—this is called the emptiness of non-requital. In that regard, what is the emptiness of intrinsic nature?

That which is the intrinsic nature of all dharmas, whether conditioned or unconditioned—that intrinsic nature is empty by its very nature, on account of its being neither immutable nor subject to destruction.
This is called the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*)?
"All phenomena" refers to...

12. Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena; visual consciousness, auditory consciousness, olfactory consciousness, gustatory consciousness, tactile consciousness, and mental consciousness; visual contact, up to mental contact, and the feeling conditioned by mental contact; material phenomena, immaterial phenomena, and conditioned and unconditioned phenomena—these are called all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). 13. [The list continues as above... These are called all phenomena.
In that regard, phenomena are empty of phenomena because they are neither immutable nor subject to destruction. For what reason? Because this is their very nature.

This is called the emptiness of all phenomena. In that regard, what is the emptiness of specific characteristics? Form has the characteristic of being formable; sensation has the characteristic of experiencing.

(AṣṭāB, Pl. I, 3/4) Recto 1: Feeling has the characteristic of experiencing; perception has the characteristic of grasping; mental formations have the characteristic of volitional construction; consciousness has the characteristic of discernment. And there is the characteristic of conditioned phenomena, as well as that of unconditioned phenomena.

2. As for the characteristic: all these phenomena (*dharmas*) are empty of their own respective characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), on account of their being neither immutable nor subject to destruction. For what reason? Because this is their very nature (*prakṛti*). In that regard, what is the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*)? Those phenomena which are past, future, or present—there is no apprehension of them, and that non-apprehension is empty by virtue of non-apprehension, on account of their being neither immutable nor subject to destruction. For what reason? Because this is their very nature. In that regard, what is the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*)? Where there is existence...
This is called the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*)? That wherein no intrinsic nature is apprehended—this is called the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
In that regard, what is the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence?

There is no intrinsic nature of any composite phenomenon because all phenomena are dependently originated; this is called the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. Existence is empty of existence; non-existence is empty of non-existence; intrinsic nature is empty of intrinsic nature.

6. Other-nature is empty of other-nature. In that regard, what is "nature"? Nature is said to be the five aggregates. Therein, the five aggregates are empty of nature because they are unarisen. Thus, nature is empty of nature. What is non-existence? How is non-existence empty of non-existence? Non-existence is said to be the unconditioned. Therein, the unconditioned is empty of the unconditioned; thus, non-existence is empty.
How is it that intrinsic nature is empty of intrinsic nature?

That which is the emptiness of all phenomena is not made by knowledge, nor made by vision, nor made by anyone at all; thus, intrinsic nature is empty of intrinsic nature. In this regard, what is the emptiness of other-nature (*parabhāvaśūnyatā*)?
It is [the state] whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise.
Or rather, it is the stability of phenomena among all phenomena, their true nature, the realm of phenomena,
the fixed order of phenomena,
and likewise the suchness that is non-other, the non-falsity, and the limit of reality.

Thus, that which is the state of these phenomena being empty of anything beyond [themselves] is called the emptiness of other-being (*parabhāva-śūnyatā*). This, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, this is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, namely:

11. The concentration named Śūraṅgama; the concentration named Ratnamudrā; the concentration named Siṃhavikrīḍita; the concentration named Sucandra; the concentration named Candradhvajaketu; the concentration named Sarvadharmodgata.

12. The concentration named Vilokitamūrdhā; the concentration named Dharmadhātuniyata; the concentration named Niyatadhvajaketu; the concentration named Vajropama; the seal for entering all phenomena (sarvadharmapraveśamudrā).

The concentration named [Nāma], 13. the concentration named Well-Established King of Concentrations (*samādhirāja-supratiṣṭhita*), the concentration named Emitted Ray (*raśmi-pramukta*), the concentration named Power and Vigor (*bala-vīrya*), the concentration named Emerged (*samudgata*), the concentration named Entry into the Certainty of Etymological Explanation (*nirukta-niyata-praveśa*), 14.

the concentration named Entry into Designations (*adhivacana-sampraveśa*), the concentration named Surveying the Directions (*dig-vilokanā*), the concentration named Seal of the Dhāraṇīs (*dhāraṇī-mudra*), the concentration named Non-Forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣa*), and the concentration named Ocean-Seal of the Convergence of All Phenomena (*sarvadharma-samavasaraṇa-sāgara-mudra*).

The concentration named Verso, the concentration named Pervading Space, the concentration named Vajra Mandala, the concentration named Abandoning Dust, the concentration named Vairocana, the concentration named Without Search, the concentration named Dwelling Without Abode,

the concentration named Thoughtless, the concentration named Stainless Lamp, the concentration named Infinite Radiance, the concentration named Light-Maker, and the concentration named Universal Illumination.
The concentration named Pure Essence;

the concentration named Stainless Radiance; the concentration named Creator of Delight; the concentration named Lamp of Lightning; the concentration named Inexhaustible; the concentration named Lord of Splendor; the concentration named Free from Decay; the concentration named Immovable.

4. The concentration named "Irreversible," the concentration named "Sun-Lamp," the concentration named "Moon-Pure," the concentration named "Pure Radiance," the concentration named "Producer of Light," and the concentration named "Form-Maker.

The concentration named "Seal of the Supreme Dharma," the concentration named "Sameness of All Dharmas," the concentration named "Abandoning Delight," the concentration named "Dharma-Exalted," the concentration named "Scattering," the concentration named "Illuminator of All Words," and the concentration named "Manifestation of Equal Syllables."

The concentration called "Nameless," the concentration called "Beyond Syllables," the concentration called "Severing of Objects," the concentration called "Without Mode," the concentration called "Unchanging," the concentration called "Wandering Without Abode";

the concentration called "Free from Darkness," the concentration called "Possessing Conduct," the concentration called "Immovable," the concentration called "Crossed Beyond the Realm," the concentration called "Attaining the Accumulation of All Virtues," the concentration called "Steadfast Mind."

The concentration named "Pure Bloom of Virtue," the concentration named "Possessing the Factors of Enlightenment," the concentration named "Infinite Eloquence," the concentration named "Unequaled," the concentration named "Transcending All Phenomena," the concentration named "Effecting Delimitation," the concentration named "Dispelling Doubt," the concentration named "Without Basis," the concentration named "Single Array," and the concentration named "Manifestation of Aspects."

The concentration named Single Aspect; the concentration named Maker of Aspects; the concentration named Shattering All Bases of Existence with Penetrating Wisdom; the concentration named Entry into Conventional Sounds; the concentration named Possessing Sound yet Liberated from Words and Syllables;
and the concentration named Blazing Torch.

The concentration named "Purification of Characteristics," the concentration named "Without Marks," the concentration named "Endowed with the Excellence of All Aspects," the concentration named "Non-Relishing of Pleasure and Pain," and the concentration named "Inexhaustible Casket. The concentration named "Basis of Dhāraṇīs," the concentration named "Devouring All Rightness and Wrongness," the concentration named "Thorough Pacification of Obstruction and Suppression," and the concentration named "Non-Obstruction and Non-Suppression."
the concentration named Vimalaprabha (Stainless Light),

the concentration named Sāravatī (Possessing Essence), the concentration named Paripūrṇacandravimala (Pure as the Full Moon), the concentration named Mahāvyūha (Great Array), the concentration named Sarvākāraprabhākara (Illuminator of All Aspects),
and the concentration named Samādhisamata (Equality of Concentrations).
(AṣṭāB, Pl. II, 1/2) Recto 1:

The concentration named "dustless and free from passion"; the concentration named "the convergence of all that is without conflict and with conflict"; [and] "delighting in the absence of support and abode."

The concentration called "the mindless abiding in suchness," the concentration called "the crushing of the defilement of body," the concentration called "the destruction of the defilement of speech, like space," and the concentration called "unattached and unstained like the sky. In that regard, what is the concentration called "śūraṅgama"?

That concentration by which one experiences the range of all concentrations is called the concentration called "śūraṅgama. In that regard, what is the concentration called "ratnamudrā"? By means of which concentration... [all concentrations...]

This is called the fourth, the samādhi named Jewel-Seal (*ratnamudra*). In that regard, what is the samādhi named Lion’s Sport (*siṃhavikrīḍita*)? That samādhi in which, having remained, one sports with all samādhis—this is called that samādhi.
In that regard, what is the samādhi named Good Moon (*sucandra*)? That samādhi in which, having remained, one illuminates all samādhis—this is called the samādhi named Good Moon. In that regard...
What is the concentration called Moon-Flag Banner?
It is that concentration in which, having remained, one holds the banner of all concentrations; this is called the concentration named Moon-Flag Banner.
In that regard, what is the concentration called Surpassing All Phenomena? It is that concentration in which, having remained, by means of all concentrations...

This is called the samādhi named "Surpassing All Phenomena. In that regard, what is the samādhi named "Surveying the Summit"? 9. This is called the concentration named "fixed in the realm of phenomena" (*dharmadhātuniyata*). In that regard, what is the concentration named "the banner of certainty" (*niyatadhvajaketu*)? The concentration in which, having remained, one upholds the banner of all concentrations—this is called the concentration named "the banner of certainty. In that regard, what is the concentration named "diamond-like" (*vajropama*)? The concentration in which, having remained, one does not shatter any concentrations—this is called the diamond-like concentration.
What is concentration therein?

The concentration called the Seal of Entry into Phenomena (*dharmapraveśamudrā*): abiding in which concentration one enters the seal of phenomena; this is called the concentration of the Seal of Entry into Phenomena. What is the concentration therein called the Well-Established King of Concentrations (*samadhirājasupratiṣṭhita*)?

12. Abiding in which concentration one becomes firmly established among all concentrations by means of the royal establishment—this is called the concentration "Well-Established King of Concentrations" (*samādhirājasupratiṣṭhita*). Therein, what is the concentration called "Emission of Rays" (*raśmipramukta*)? Abiding in which concentration one emits rays from all concentrations—this is called the concentration "Emission of Rays. Therein, what is the concentration called "Powerful Vigor" (*balavīrya*)? Abiding in which concentration...
Abiding in all meditative concentrations, one maintains power and vigor;

this is called the meditative concentration named "Power and Vigor. In that regard, what is the meditative concentration named "Exalted" (*samudgata*)? It is that meditative concentration in which, for one who abides therein, all meditative concentrations emerge; this is called "Exalted."

Verse 1: Regarding that, what is the samādhi of entry into the exposition of etymological definitions? It is the samādhi in which, having abided, one enters into the exposition of the etymological definitions of samādhis; this is called the samādhi of entry into the exposition of etymological definitions. Regarding that:

2. What is the concentration called "entry into designations" (*adhivacana-saṃpraveśa*)? That concentration in which, having remained, one enters into the designations and names of all concentrations—this is called the concentration of entry into designations. Therein, what is the concentration called "surveying the directions" (*digvilokanā*)? That concentration in which, having remained, one surveys the directions of all concentrations—this is called the concentration of surveying the directions. Therein, what is the concentration called "the seal of retention" (*dhāraṇīmudra*)?

There is the concentration called the Seal of Retention (*dhāraṇīmudra*); abiding in this concentration, one maintains the seal of all concentrations—this is called the concentration named the Seal of Retention.
In that regard, what is the concentration called Non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣa*)? Abiding in which concentration, [one maintains] all concentrations...

One does not forget it; this is called the concentration of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣa-samādhi*). In that regard, what is the ocean-seal concentration (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*) which is the convergence of all phenomena? It is that concentration wherein, by abiding in which, all concentrations reach a state of inclusion and convergence; this is so called.

6. The *samādhi* called the "Seal of the Ocean in Which All Dharmas Converge. In that regard, what is the *samādhi* called "Pervading Space"? It is the state wherein, by abiding in this *samādhi*, one pervades all *samādhis* with the quality of pervading space; this is called the *samādhi* "Pervading Space. In that regard, what is the *samādhi* called "Vajra Mandala"? It is the state wherein, by abiding in this *samādhi*, one maintains the mandala of all *samādhis*; this is called [the *samādhi*] "Vajra Mandala."

The vajra-maṇḍala samādhi. Therein, what is the samādhi called "the abandonment of dust"? That samādhi in which, having remained, one abandons all signs of the afflictions—this is called the samādhi "abandonment of dust. Therein, what is the samādhi called "Vairocana"?

9. That concentration by abiding in which one illuminates all concentrations is called the concentration named Vairocana. Therein, what is the concentration named Aneṣa? That concentration by abiding in which one does not seek any phenomenon within concentration is called the Aneṣa concentration. Therein, what is the concentration of dwelling without a home? That concentration in which one does not perceive any phenomenon as dwelling in a home.

This is called the concentration of dwelling without a home (aniketasthita-samādhi). In that regard, what is the concentration without thought (niścitta-samādhi)? It is that concentration in which neither the mind nor mental factors (caitasika-dharma) operate; this is called the concentration without thought. In that regard, what is the concentration named the stainless lamp (vimalapradīpa-samādhi)? In that concentration...
12. This which makes a stainless lamp of all meditative concentrations is called the "Stainless Lamp" (*vimalapradīpa*) concentration.

Therein, what is the "Infinite Radiance" (*anantaprabha*) concentration? That concentration in which, having abided, one produces infinite radiance; this is called the concentration named "Infinite Radiance. 13. Therein, what is the concentration named "Light-Maker" (*prabhākara*)? That concentration in which, having abided, one produces light for all phenomena; this is called the "Light-Maker" concentration.

In that regard, what is the *samantāvabhāsa* (all-illuminating) concentration? Upon the simultaneous attainment of this concentration, all gateways of concentration are illuminated; this is called the *samantāvabhāsa* concentration. In that regard, what is the *samadhiśuddhasāra* (pure essence) concentration? [One folio is missing]

He transcends this; this is called the concentration named "Crossing Over the Object. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Attaining the Accumulation of All Qualities"?

It is that wherein one attains the accumulation of qualities of all phenomena and all concentrations; this is called the concentration "Attaining the Accumulation of All Qualities. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Stable Mind"? It is that wherein—
