Abiding in which samādhi one attains the purity of the blooming flowers of all samādhis—this is called the "samādhi of the purity of blooming flowers. In that regard, what is the "bodhy-aṅgavatī (possessing the factors of enlightenment) samādhi"? Abiding in which samādhi [one attains] from all samādhis the seven...

This is called the concentration possessing the factors of enlightenment. In that regard, what is the concentration of infinite eloquence? It is that wherein one attains infinite eloquence regarding all concentrations;

this is called the concentration of infinite eloquence. In that regard, what is the unequaled concentration? It is that concentration wherein, having stood, one attains the state of being unequaled with respect to all concentrations; this is called the unequaled concentration. In that regard, what is...

The concentration called "Transcending All" is that concentration by remaining in which one transcends the entire triple world; this is called the concentration of transcending all phenomena (*sarvadharmātikramaṇa-samādhi*). In that regard, what is the concentration called "Distinguishing"?

It is that concentration by remaining in which one perceives the distinction between all phenomena and all concentrations; this is called the concentration of distinguishing. In that regard, what is the concentration called "Dispelling Doubt"?

There is a concentration called "the disperser of doubt," wherein one attains the dispersal of doubt regarding all concentrations; this is called the concentration that disperses doubt. In that regard, what is the concentration called "without basis"? It is that concentration wherein, having abided, one does not perceive the location of any phenomena.

10. This is called the "unsupported" (*niradhiṣṭhāna*) samādhi. In that regard, what is the samādhi called "single array" (*ekavyūha*)? It is that samādhi in which, having remained, one does not perceive duality in any phenomenon;

this is called the "single array" samādhi. 11. In that regard, what is the samādhi called "accomplishment of aspects" (*ākārābhinirhāra*)? It is that samādhi in which, having remained, one does not perceive the accomplishment of the aspects of all phenomena; this is indeed called the "accomplishment of aspects."

What is concentration? Therein, what is the concentration called "single aspect"? It is that concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive the aspect of any concentrations; this is called the concentration of single aspect. Therein, what is the concentration that "produces aspects"? It is that concentration in which, having remained, one perceives the non-duality of all concentrations; this is called the concentration that produces aspects. Therein, what is the concentration that "pierces and shatters the entire foundation of existence"?

There is a concentration called "the piercer," by abiding in which concentration one enters into the piercing knowledge of all concentrations; through the entry into which one does not perceive any phenomenon whatsoever— this is called "the disperser of the base of all existence through piercing."

1. In that regard, what is the *samādhi* called "Entry into Conventional Sounds"? It is the concentration in which, having remained, one enters into the conventional sounds of all *samādhis*; this is called the *samādhi* "Entry into Conventional Sounds. In that regard, what is the *samādhi* named "Free from Vocal Sound and Syllables"? It is the concentration in which, having remained, one perceives all *samādhis* as being free from vocal sound and syllables; this is called the *samādhi* "Free from Vocal Sound and Syllables."

In that regard, what is the *jvalanolkā* concentration? That concentration in which, having remained, one illuminates all concentrations with splendor—this is called the *jvalanolkā* concentration. In that regard, what is the concentration named *lakṣaṇapariśodhana* (purification of characteristics), in which...

4. Abiding in this samādhi, the characteristics of all samādhis become completely purified; this is called the "characteristics-purifying" (lakṣaṇapariśodhana) samādhi. In that regard, what is the samādhi called "unmarked" (anabhilakṣa)? It is that samādhi in which, having abided, one perceives all samādhis as unmarked; this is called the "unmarked" samādhi. In that regard, what is the "endowed with the excellence of all aspects" (sarvākāravaropeta) samādhi? It is that samādhi in which, for one who has abided, all samādhis are endowed with the excellence of all aspects.

6. This is called the concentration endowed with the excellence of all aspects. In that regard, what is the concentration of non-delight in pleasure and pain? It is that concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive pleasure or pain in any concentrations; this is called the concentration named "non-delight in pleasure and pain. In that regard, what is the concentration named "inexhaustible aspect"? It is that concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive the exhaustion of concentrations. This is it.
It is said: "The concentration of the aspect of imperishability.

Therein, what is the concentration called the "basis of retention" (*dhāraṇīpada*)? That concentration in which, having remained, one retains all retentions—this is called the concentration of the basis of retention. Therein, what is the concentration called "the total devouring of rightness and wrongness"?
That concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive the rightness or wrongness of any concentrations.

This is called the concentration that completely devours both correctness and falsity. In this regard, what is the concentration named "the pacification of obstruction and cessation"? It is that concentration in which, having remained, one thoroughly perceives the obstruction and cessation of all concentrations; this is called the concentration "the pacification of obstruction and cessation. In this regard, what is the concentration "non-opposition and non-obstruction"?

11. The concentration in which, having remained, one perceives the non-opposition and non-obstruction of all concentrations—this is called the concentration of non-opposition and non-obstruction. Among those, what is the concentration named Vimalaprabha? In which concentration, having remained, one does not perceive the circle of light of any concentration—this is called the Vimalaprabha concentration. Among those, what is the Sāravatī concentration? In which concentration...

Abiding [in this], one perceives the lack of essence in all meditative absorptions; this is called the "Essential" (*sāravatī*) absorption. In that regard, what is the "Stainless Full Moon" (*paripūrṇacandravimala*) absorption? It is that absorption in which all meditative absorptions become completely full, just as on the fifteenth day [of the lunar month].

14. This is called the moon-disk, the "Stainless Full Moon" samādhi. In that regard, what is the samādhi called "Great Array" (*mahāvyūha*), by abiding in which samādhi all samādhis are endowed with the Great Array?
(AṣṭāB, Pl. III, 1/2) Recto.
This is called the Mahāvyūha (Great Array) samādhi. In that regard, what is the samādhi called Sarvākāraprabhākara (Illuminator of All Aspects)?
It is that samādhi in which, having remained, one illuminates all samādhis and all dharmas; this is called Sarvākāraprabhākara.

2. What is the concentration of the equality of concentrations? It is that concentration in which, having remained, one perceives the non-distraction and one-pointedness of all concentrations; this is called the concentration of the equality of concentrations. 3. What is the concentration free from dust? It is that in which one makes all concentrations free from afflictions (*kleśa*); this is called the concentration free from dust. What is the concentration that is the convergence of all that is without strife and with strife?

4. There is a concentration called "the one in which all concentrations do not conflict. When one is established in this concentration, no concentrations clash; this is called the concentration that is the convergence of all non-conflicting and conflicting concentrations. In that regard, what is the concentration called "delighting in the absence of a basis or abode"?

It is the concentration in which one does not enter the storehouse (ālaya) of any concentrations; this is called the concentration "delighting in the absence of a basis or abode. In that regard, what is the concentration called "mindless and established in suchness"? [It is the concentration] in which...

The suchness (*tathatā*) of all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) does not turn back; this is called the "meditative absorption of non-mind fixed in suchness. In that regard, what is the meditative absorption called "the crushing of the defilement of body"? It is that meditative absorption wherein, having remained, one does not perceive the body of any meditative absorption; this is called the meditative absorption called "the crushing of the defilement of body. In that regard, what is the meditative absorption called "like space, destroying the defilement of speech"? It is that meditative absorption wherein...

Abiding in all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), one does not perceive verbal action; this is called the "space-like meditative concentration that destroys the defilement of speech. In that regard, what is the meditative concentration called "unstained and liberated from attachment to space"? It is that meditative concentration in which one attains the state of being unstained by all phenomena; this is called the "unstained and liberated-from-attachment-to-space meditative concentration. Subhūti, this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s [practice] in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
The fifteenth chapter, titled "The Practice of the Mahāyāna," concerning Samādhi.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is as follows:
11. Namely, the four foundations of mindfulness. In that regard, what is the foundation of mindfulness of the body?
Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body in the internal body;
yet he does not [cling to] those things associated with the body...

12. Ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, he dwells contemplating the body in the external body; he dwells contemplating the body in both the internal and external body, yet he does not dwell contemplating thoughts directed toward the body.

13. Ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, he dwells contemplating feelings in internal feelings, the mind in the mind, and phenomena in phenomena.
He dwells ardent,

clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world; observing external phenomena, he dwells ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
He dwells ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
How, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell contemplating the body in the internal body?
Here, Subhūti,

2. A bodhisattva mahāsattva, while walking, knows: "I am walking. While standing, he knows: "I am standing. While sitting, he knows: "I am sitting. While lying down, he knows: "I am lying down. Furthermore, in whatever way his body is positioned, he knows it exactly as it is. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body within the body, ardent...

4. Possessing mindfulness, he has subdued covetousness and dejection regarding the world. Furthermore, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva acts with clear comprehension in going out and coming back; he acts with clear comprehension in looking ahead and looking aside. He acts with clear comprehension in carrying his outer robe, alms bowl, and robes; in eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; in lying down, sleeping, and waking; in coming and going, standing and sitting, sleeping and being awake, speaking and remaining silent, and in wise withdrawal into seclusion.

6. He acts with clear comprehension. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells contemplating the body in the internal body, and that by way of non-apprehension.
7. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, breathes in mindfully and breathes out mindfully; he breathes in long or breathes out long.

8. He discerns: "I am breathing out long; I am breathing in long; I am breathing in long; I am breathing out long. Or he breathes in short; he discerns: "I am breathing in short. Or he breathes out short; he discerns:
"I am breathing out short. Subhūti, it is just as, for example, a potter or a potter's apprentice [discerns the length of his breath].

Or, when breathing out long, he clearly knows, "I am breathing out long"; or, when breathing in short, having pierced [the breath] short, he clearly knows, "I am piercing [the breath] short. In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being mindful while inhaling and mindful while exhaling: when breathing in long, he clearly knows, "I am breathing in long. When breathing in long... [he knows,] "I am breathing in long."
Exhaling long, he discerns, "I am exhaling long"; inhaling short, he discerns, "I am inhaling short"; exhaling short, he discerns, "I am exhaling short.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body within the internal body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva...

He contemplates this very body by way of its elements: "In this [body] there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element. Subhūti, it is just as if a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice were to slaughter a cow with a sharp blade.
“Just as one who, having killed a cow, should cut it into four portions, and having cut it into four portions, examines them while standing or sitting—just so, Subhūti, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
[One folio missing] (AṣṭāB, Pl. III, 3/4)

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees on a charnel ground bones of many colors— blue, pigeon-colored, or reduced to dust, leveled with the soil and the earth— he [compares] this very body [to them].
He applies it there [as follows]: "This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a kind; indeed, it is not exempt from this very condition.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body in the internal body, in the external body, and in the internal-external body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful. Likewise, he dwells contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful. This, Subhūti, is also the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore...

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is this: namely, the four right efforts. What are the four? Here, Subhūti, for the sake of the non-arising of evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen, a bodhisattva...

5. He generates desire, exerts himself, upholds the mind, and correctly applies himself for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have arisen; he generates desire, strives, exerts himself, and correctly applies his mind for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have arisen. 6. He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, upholds the mind, and correctly applies himself for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen; he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, upholds the mind, and correctly applies himself for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen. 7. [He generates desire, exerts himself, upholds the mind, and correctly applies himself] for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, expansion, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have already arisen.

For the stability of wholesome dharmas, for their further increase, for their non-forgetfulness, for their non-decline, and for their fulfillment, he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses vigor, takes hold of the mind, and correctly applies it. Subhūti, this too is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of these four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

9. What are the four? Here, Subhūti, one cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of abandonment and concentration of desire; it is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment. 10. One cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of abandonment and concentration of energy; one cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of abandonment and concentration of mind; [one cultivates] the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of abandonment and concentration of investigation.

One cultivates the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) which are based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and result in relinquishment; and that by way of non-apprehension. Subhūti, this too is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, the five faculties (pañcendriya). Which five?
Namely, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

The faculty of wisdom. This too, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. And that, moreover, by way of non-apprehension. Furthermore, Subhūti, the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is this, namely: the five powers. What are the five? The power of faith, the power of vigor, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. This too, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
And that is by way of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva consists of the seven factors of enlightenment.

What are these seven? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena; and the factors of enlightenment that are energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—each based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment—and all this by way of non-apprehension. This, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is this: namely, the noble eightfold path. What is the noble eightfold path? It is right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right effort.
Right mindfulness and right concentration, and that by way of non-apprehension.

This too, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is this: namely, the three concentrations that are gateways to liberation. What are the three? The concentration of emptiness, the signless concentration, and the wishless concentration. Among these, what is...

For one who contemplates empty phenomena, there is the gate of liberation that is emptiness; for one who contemplates signless phenomena, there is the gate of liberation that is the signless; and for one who contemplates the non-conditioning of formative forces, there is the gate of liberation that is wishlessness. Subhūti, this too is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. One should train in these three gates of liberation. Furthermore, Subhūti, for the bodhisattva mahāsattva...

The Mahāyāna consists, namely, of eleven knowledges (*jñāna*). What are the eleven? They are: the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)—and so forth, as in the formula—up to the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Regarding what was stated as "knowledge," therein, which is [the knowledge of others' minds]?

10. What is the knowledge of suffering? It is the knowledge of the non-arising of suffering; this is called the knowledge of suffering. In that regard, what is the knowledge of origin? It is the knowledge of the abandonment of origin. What is the knowledge of cessation? It is the knowledge of the cessation of suffering. 11. What is the knowledge of the path? It is the knowledge of the noble eightfold path. What is the knowledge of exhaustion? It is the knowledge of the exhaustion of lust, hatred, and delusion. What is the knowledge of non-arising? It is that which...
What is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?

It is the knowledge that discerns the five aggregates as lacking intrinsic nature (*aprakṛti*). What is subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)? It is the knowledge that "the eye is impermanent; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are impermanent," and so on, up to "phenomena are impermanent."

13. Knowledge up to the knowledge that dependent origination is impermanent—this is called subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). What is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*)? It is the knowledge, by means of one's own mind, of the minds and mental factors of other sentient beings and other persons.

14. What is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*)? It is the knowledge of the path (*pratipad-jñāna*). What is the knowledge as it has been taught (*yathokta-jñāna*)? It is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the omniscience of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā-jñāna*). Subhūti, this too belongs to the bodhisattva.
The Mahāyāna of the Mahāsattva (Aṣṭādaśasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, Plate IV, 1/2), recto.
And that is by way of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is this: namely, the three faculties. What are the three? They are the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowing, and the faculty of one who has known.

Therein, what is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"? It is the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, and the faculty of concentration belonging to those persons who have not yet attained the trainings.
Regarding the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), what therein is the faculty of having known (*ājñendriya*)?

It is the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom belonging to those persons in training (*śaikṣa*) who have already attained full knowledge; this is called the faculty of having known.
What therein is the faculty of one who has fully known (*ājñātāvīndriya*)?

4. That which is the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom belonging to those persons who are beyond training—namely, Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas—5.
this is called the faculty of one who has already known. This too, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, and that is by way of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of these three concentrations. What are the three? They are: concentration with applied thought and sustained thought; concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only; and concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought. Among these, concentration with applied thought and sustained thought is the first dhyāna: secluded from sensual desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome states, accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and born of seclusion, it is rapture and happiness.

This is called concentration with applied thought and sustained thought (savitarkaḥ savicāraḥ samādhiḥ). In that regard, what is concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only (avitarko vicāramātraḥ samādhiḥ)? It is said to be the interval between the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna; this is called concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only.
In that regard, what is...?

9. "The concentration free from applied thought and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra-samādhi*). From the second dhyāna up to that which is called 'neither perception nor non-perception'—this too, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. 10. Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, the ten recollections (*daśānusmṛti*). What are the ten? They are as follows: recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), recollection of the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*), and recollection of the Saṅgha (*saṃghānusmṛti*)."

11. The recollection of renunciation, the recollection of the deities, the recollection of agitation, the recollection directed toward the body, the recollection of inhalation and exhalation, and the recollection of death—Subhūti, this too is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, and that is by way of non-apprehension. Furthermore, Subhūti, the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, and the nine successive meditative attainments.
This too, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, and that is by way of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is this: namely, the ten powers of a Tathāgata. What are the ten? Here, a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands, as it truly is, the possible as possible regarding persons.

He understands as it really is what is impossible as impossible; he understands as it really is the ripening of past, future, and present actions and the undertaking of actions according to their basis. He understands as it really is the manifold elements and the diversity of elements.

He understands the world as it truly is; he understands, as it truly is, the diversity of inclinations among other beings and other persons. He understands, as it truly is, the superior and inferior faculties of other beings and other persons.

He understands, as it truly is, the path leading everywhere. [He understands] the factors of enlightenment, meditations, liberations, concentrations, attainments, afflictions, and purifications of other beings and other persons.

For, by virtue of ultimate purity, suchness is not apprehended; the limit of reality is not apprehended, for it is by virtue of ultimate purity that the inconceivable realm of phenomena is not apprehended;

by virtue of ultimate purity, the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields are not apprehended; by virtue of ultimate purity, dependent origination is not apprehended; and likewise, the perfection of generosity is not apprehended.

The perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom are not apprehended, by reason of their absolute purity; internal emptiness is not apprehended, by reason of its absolute purity—and so on, until—emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature is not apprehended, by reason of its absolute purity; the applications of mindfulness are not apprehended, by reason of their absolute purity.

The factors conducive to enlightenment, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha; the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, the pratyekabuddha, and the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—these are not apprehended. Indeed, this is because of their absolute purity. Likewise, the fruit of stream-entry—and so on, up to omniscience—is not apprehended, because of its absolute purity. For, by virtue of ultimate purity, there is likewise no cessation, no affliction, no purification, and no formative activity; for, by virtue of ultimate purity, a prior limit is not apprehended. For, by virtue of ultimate purity, likewise a subsequent limit is not apprehended; and for, by virtue of ultimate purity, coming, going, staying, passing away, and rebirth are not apprehended. No increase is perceived, because of its ultimate purity. Due to the non-perception of what? Everything is not perceived;

As long as the Tathāgata is not apprehended, he is not apprehended; because the fruit of stream-entry is not apprehended, he is not apprehended; up to and including because omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is not apprehended, he is not apprehended; because non-arising (*anutpāda*) is not apprehended, he is not apprehended—thus it is on the reverse side.

Non-activity is not apprehended. Because the prior limit is not apprehended, it is not apprehended; up to growth, it is not apprehended because it is not apprehended; up to the tenth stage, it is not apprehended because the first stage is not apprehended. Furthermore, the ten stages are not apprehended because the stages themselves are not apprehended. What are the ten? They are as follows: the stage of bright insight (*śuklavipaśyanā-bhūmi*), the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*), the stage of the eighth person (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*), the stage of refinement (*tanū-bhūmi*), the stage of freedom from passion (*vītarāga-bhūmi*), the stage of one who has done what was to be done (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*), the stage of the solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha-bhūmi*), the stage of the bodhisattva (*bodhisattva-bhūmi*), and the stage of the perfectly awakened one (*saṃbuddha-bhūmi*).

In that regard, within internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), the first stage (*bhūmi*) is not apprehended. The non-apprehension of the first stage is neither apprehended nor non-apprehended; and so on, until: the non-apprehension of the tenth stage is [neither apprehended nor non-apprehended], by virtue of its absolute purity. Śāradvatīputra said: "In the future time, in the final age, at the time of the disappearance of the true Dharma, there will be many noble sons or noble daughters belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle in that northern direction; however, those who [will study] this profound perfection of wisdom will be few indeed."
Having heard it, they will have faith; having had faith, they will write it down and cause it to be written down;
likewise, they will take it up, retain it, and master it.
They will recite it, teach it, speak it, attend to it with wise reflection, cultivate it, and practice in accordance with suchness.
Furthermore, having heard this profound perfection of wisdom being spoken, they will not shrink back, nor will they become dejected;
they will not be terrified, nor will they tremble, nor will they fall into a state of panic.

For what reason? Because those sons of good family or daughters of good family have followed after the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and having approached this very profound perfection of wisdom, they have questioned and interrogated them.

For what reason? They will become fully perfected in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; they will be fully perfected in the applications of mindfulness, and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Why is that? Because those sons of good family or daughters of good family will be supported by roots of virtue.
"They will act for the benefit of many people and for their happiness, starting from this very unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. For what reason?

It is because, Śāradvatīputra, I have spoken to them discourses associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones who existed in the past time also [spoke] to those sons of good family or daughters of good family discourses associated with the knowledge of all aspects.
Even when they have passed away from that birth, the same discourse will continue to be their mode of conduct— namely, concerning unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening— and furthermore,
they will themselves speak that very same discourse to others, namely, concerning unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Furthermore, those sons of good family or daughters of good family will be united and harmonious in their pursuit of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Neither Māra nor the deities belonging to Māra’s host will be able to break them apart from that unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, let alone others—those of evil intent and evil conduct; it is impossible for them to cause a division. This is not possible.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, those sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, having heard this profound perfection of wisdom, will attain sublime joy, serene confidence, and gladness,

If his giving were limited by measure, it would not be so; but because his giving is not limited by measure, it becomes the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
In this way indeed, friend Pūrṇa, a bodhisattva should give a gift that is boundless; it should not be bound by measure,
and thus it should be relinquished.
